title: Chen, Traditionalising Chinese Law — symbolic epistemic violence in the late Qing

1.title: The question the article turns around
1.text: For a whole century China has undertaken legal reforms in order to establish a 'MODERN' legal order — and commentators and scholars to this day find the Chinese system lacking elements they regard as indispensable to modern law. The unsatisfactory outcome is usually attributed to the INCOMMENSURABILITY BETWEEN CHINESE TRADITION AND MODERN VALUES as represented since the 19th century by the industrial Western countries. Underneath lies a WIDESPREAD ASSUMPTION THAT THERE ARE NATURAL BOUNDARIES BETWEEN 'TRADITIONAL' AND 'MODERN' LAW AND BETWEEN CHINESE AND WESTERN LAW. Chen turns the question around: INSTEAD OF ASKING WHETHER CHINA HAS MANAGED TO MODERNISE ITS LAW, IT IS MORE FRUITFUL TO EXAMINE HOW AND WHY THE CHINESE LEGAL ORDER CAME TO BE LABELLED TRADITIONAL IN THE FIRST PLACE — and therefore supposedly incompatible with Western and modern law. The late Qing reform of 1902–1911 is the ideal example of HOW CHINESE LAW BECAME THE TRADITIONAL, INFERIOR 'OTHER' OF BOTH WESTERN AND MODERN LAW. Three questions: 1) HOW WAS CHINESE LAW ORIENTALISED OR SELF-ORIENTALISED and made incompatible with modern law? 2) HOW DID THE CHINESE NEGOTIATE with Euro-American concepts of tradition and modernity? 3) HOW DID THE REFORM PROJECT CHALLENGE, OR CONTRIBUTE TO, THE TRADITIONALISATION (CHUANTONG HUA) OF CHINESE LAW?

terms.def: The process by which Chinese law was labelled 'traditional', and thereby made the inferior opposite of modern and Western law.

cards.q: What question does Chen ask in place of the usual question about the success of modernisation?
cards.a: Instead of asking WHETHER China has managed to modernise its law, he examines HOW AND WHY THE CHINESE LEGAL ORDER CAME TO BE LABELLED TRADITIONAL in the first place — and thereby incompatible with modern law. He thus challenges the widespread assumption that there are natural boundaries between 'traditional' and 'modern' and between Chinese and Western law.

2.title: Symbolic epistemic violence
2.text: Chen's central concept, composed of two sources. 'EPISTEMIC VIOLENCE' comes from GAYATRI SPIVAK; 'SYMBOLIC VIOLENCE' from PIERRE BOURDIEU, who understands it as 'VIOLENCE EXERCISED UPON A SOCIAL AGENT WITH HIS OR HER COMPLICITY'. By joining them Chen wants to stress TWO THINGS AT ONCE: the NORMATIVE AND EPISTEMIC PRESSURE THAT DOMINANT CULTURES AND DISCOURSES EXERTED ON THE CHINESE CONCEPTION OF LEGAL MODERNITY — and, on the other side, THE CONTRIBUTION OF CHINESE ACTORS TO 'PRODUCING THE EFFICACY' OF THOSE DISCOURSES. His purpose is in part to point out that THE CHINESE THEMSELVES TOOK PART IN THE TRADITIONALISATION OR ORIENTALISATION OF CHINESE LAW AND CULTURE. And a methodological point Chen emphasises: REAL OR PERCEIVED DIFFERENCES BETWEEN TWO CULTURES, CIVILISATIONS OR LEGAL ORDERS DO NOT AND SHOULD NOT MEAN INCOMMENSURABILITY OR HIERARCHY BETWEEN THEM — UNLESS PEOPLE CHOOSE TO INVEST THOSE DIFFERENCES WITH NORMATIVE, IDEOLOGICAL MEANING.

terms.def: Spivak and Bourdieu combined: the normative pressure of dominant discourses plus the complicity of the subjected themselves in 'producing their efficacy'.

cards.q: What does 'symbolic epistemic violence' mean and why does Chen combine the two concepts?
cards.a: 'Epistemic violence' comes from Spivak, 'symbolic violence' from Bourdieu — 'violence exercised upon a social agent WITH HIS OR HER COMPLICITY'. By combining them he wants to stress both at once: the pressure of dominant discourses on the Chinese conception of legal modernity AND the contribution of Chinese actors themselves to 'producing the efficacy' of those discourses.

cards.q: When does a difference between cultures turn into a hierarchy?
cards.a: Only when people CHOOSE to INVEST that difference WITH NORMATIVE, IDEOLOGICAL MEANING. Difference between cultures, civilisations or legal orders does not and should not by itself mean incommensurability or hierarchy — the story of the traditionalisation of Chinese law is the example.

3.title: China as a mirror of the European Enlightenment
3.text: The reform cannot be understood merely from the wish to abolish extraterritoriality, nor merely from the context of the Opium Wars — it belongs to a longer time frame and to the global history of cross-cultural encounters, modernity, colonialism and orientalism which PRECEDED IT BY TWO OR THREE CENTURIES. Western knowledge of China and of Chinese law grew from the 16th to the 19th century through the work of missionaries, diplomats and early sinologists — among them SIR GEORGE THOMAS STAUNTON, who in 1810 published THE FIRST ENGLISH TRANSLATION OF THE QING CODE (without most of the sub-statutes). And that knowledge played an important role BOTH AS POSITIVE INSPIRATION AND AS NEGATIVE FOIL in shaping the debates about modernity in the West: MONTESQUIEU, VOLTAIRE, BECCARIA AND BENTHAM all engaged, explicitly or tacitly, with the 'CHINESE CIPHER' as a key reference point in developing their theories of the modern legal and political system. Their influential writings on the rule of law, rational and humane criminal justice and systematic codification stimulated an interest in reform from the late 18th century onwards — AND THE DISCOURSE OF LEGAL MODERNITY ITSELF WAS SOON DEPLOYED AS THE MASTER NARRATIVE HELPING TO LEGITIMISE WESTERN COLONIAL EXPANSION AS A CIVILISING MISSION IN THE EAST.

cards.q: What role did China play in the emergence of the European discourse of legal modernity?
cards.a: The role of both POSITIVE INSPIRATION AND NEGATIVE FOIL. Montesquieu, Voltaire, Beccaria and Bentham engaged with the 'Chinese cipher' as a key reference point in developing their theories of the modern legal and political system — and their writings on the rule of law, rational justice and codification stimulated a reformist interest whose discourse then served to legitimise colonial expansion as a civilising mission.

4.title: Extraterritoriality first, justification afterwards
4.text: This is Chen's sharpest thesis and it is worth knowing precisely. THE DESIRE OF THE EUROPEAN EMPIRES FOR EXTRATERRITORIALITY IN THE EAST GAVE RISE TO A GLOBAL DISCOURSE ABOUT CHINA AS AN ORIENTAL DESPOTISM RULED BY A BACKWARD TRADITION OF ARBITRARY, IRRATIONAL AND BARBARIC LAWS. It was fed by widely circulated sensational accounts of Sino-Western legal disputes and by unforgettable images of real or supposed Chinese judicial brutality in the 18th and 19th centuries. And then the treaties did their work: THE SERIES OF UNEQUAL TREATIES SIGNED AFTER THE FIRST OPIUM WAR, WHICH GRANTED THE POWERS EXTRATERRITORIAL PRIVILEGES, CONFIRMED AND CODIFIED THOSE EARLIER WESTERN PORTRAYALS OF CHINESE LAW AS INCOMMENSURABLE WITH THE LAW OF 'CIVILISED' NATIONS. By 1900 the Euro-American discourse of modern law and the orientalist discourse about China had merged into the DOMINANT DISCOURSE OF LEGAL MODERNITY in late Qing China. And the key correction of the traditional account: CONTRARY TO THE ACCEPTED VIEW IN MODERN HISTORIOGRAPHY, THE DEMAND OF BRITAIN AND THE OTHER POWERS FOR EXTRATERRITORIALITY HAD PRACTICALLY NOTHING TO DO WITH THE CHINESE LEGAL ORDER ITSELF; THE POWERS NEVERTHELESS JUSTIFIED IT BY PORTRAYING CHINESE LAW AS UNCIVILISED.

cards.q: Was the demand for extraterritoriality connected with the actual state of Chinese law?
cards.a: PRACTICALLY NOT — Chen states this expressly against the accepted view of historiography. The powers wanted extraterritoriality for other reasons but JUSTIFIED IT BY PORTRAYING CHINESE LAW AS UNCIVILISED. The unequal treaties after the First Opium War then CONFIRMED AND CODIFIED that image of incommensurability.

5.title: The two cases that set it off
5.text: Chen shows the shift in Chinese self-understanding through two causes célèbres of the 1870s, as followed by the Shanghai paper SHENBAO (1872–1949) and the English NORTH CHINA HERALD. In 1873 the actor YANG YUELOU was convicted in Shanghai UNDER JUDICIAL TORTURE of abducting the daughter of a Cantonese comprador. In 1875–1876 YANG NAIWU and XIAO BAICAI ('Little Cabbage') of Zhejiang were likewise forced to confess to adultery and to the murder of her husband; their death sentences were reversed after the EMPRESS DOWAGER CIXI intervened and ordered a retrial in Beijing. And now the rhetoric: in Yang's case the North China Herald saw further 'PROOF THAT THE CHINESE — THE MANDARINS AT LEAST — SCARCELY DESERVE CREDIT FOR BEING HALF-CIVILISED', and half a year later concluded: 'WHATEVER THE MERITS OF THE CASE, THE MERE BRUTALITY OF THE PROCEEDINGS IS ENOUGH TO RELEGATE THE VAUNTED CIVILISATION OF CHINA TO THE CATEGORY OF BARBARISM.' In other words: REGARDLESS OF THE LEGAL OR FACTUAL BASIS OF THE PROCEEDINGS, THE WAY CHINA ADMINISTERED LAW MADE THE COUNTRY A BARBARIC ONE. Shenbao, by contrast, did not reject the whole system but appropriated foreign ideas to call for reform.

cards.q: How did the British press interpret the Chinese judicial causes célèbres of the 1870s?
cards.a: As proof of barbarism regardless of the merits: the North China Herald wrote that 'whatever the merits of the case, the mere brutality of the proceedings is enough to relegate the vaunted civilisation of China to the category of barbarism' — and that the Chinese scarcely deserve credit for being half-civilised. The Yang Yuelou and Yang Naiwu cases were then cited as proof that the Chinese system was unfit to govern people of civilised nations.

6.title: Shenbao: legal reform before technology, and Turkey as a warning
6.text: A Shenbao editorial of early 1876 argued that the glaring failings of the judges showed that the government must find more effective ways of enforcing the laws in force and improve the procedures of adjudication if it was serious about its mission to 'CHERISH HUMAN LIVES' (AIXI MINMING). And it came up with an order of priority worth remembering: JUDICIAL REFORM SHOULD TAKE PRECEDENCE OVER THE INTRODUCTION OF WESTERN SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY — with TURKEY as the cautionary example. TURKEY'S IMPORT OF NEW EUROPEAN TECHNOLOGY AND MACHINERY DID NOT PREVENT FOREIGN DOMINATION, BECAUSE THE COUNTRY CLUNG TO 'ASIATIC CUSTOMS' (YAXIYA CHENGXI) AND DID NOT REFORM ITS LEGAL ORDER. 'NOTHING WILL AVAIL IF THE PEOPLE ARE NOT GIVEN PROPER LEGAL PROTECTION OR GUIDANCE.' But those commentaries also show a second thing: THE OVERRATING OF THE WEST. The same editors recommended adopting elements of European criminal justice because European judicial systems supposedly 'NEVER LEAD TO WRONGFUL CONVICTIONS NOR LET THE GUILTY ESCAPE'. And an overestimation of Western lawyers led Shenbao in 1873 and 1880 to claim that the lack of such professionals was a serious defect of Chinese justice: against the Chinese LITIGATION MASTERS (SONGGUN), censured for stirring up petty disputes, forging evidence and colluding with clerks, stood Western lawyers praised for expertise, impartiality and fearless advocacy. Lawyers, it was said, would help to eliminate judicial torture used to extract confessions and would enable judges to decide 'ALWAYS STRICTLY' according to law and evidence.

cards.q: Why did Shenbao put legal reform before the import of technology, and with what example?
cards.a: With TURKEY: its import of European technology and machinery did not prevent foreign domination, because it clung to 'Asiatic customs' and did not reform its legal order. 'Nothing will avail if the people are not given proper legal protection or guidance.' For China to follow the Western 'path to prosperity' and avoid Turkey's fate, it had to reform its law.

cards.q: How did Shenbao overrate Western law?
cards.a: It claimed that European judicial systems 'never lead to wrongful convictions nor let the guilty escape', and praised Western lawyers for expertise, impartiality and fearless advocacy as against the Chinese litigation masters (songgun). Lawyers, it said, would eliminate torture used to extract confessions and make it possible to decide always strictly by law and evidence.

7.title: What the foreign press did not print: British law at the same time
7.text: Chen's best irony. WHAT WAS SCARCELY MENTIONED IN THE FOREIGN PRESS AND WHAT CHINESE COMMENTATORS DID NOT KNOW: THE ARBITRARINESS OF CRIMINAL JUSTICE, RAMPANT PERJURY BY JURORS AND EXCESSIVE JUDICIAL DISCRETION LED BRITISH REFORMERS BETWEEN 1810 AND 1830 TO CALL FOR CODIFICATION. And the ensuing legislative debates often came down to the question WHETHER THE PROPOSED REFORMS SUITED THE LEGAL AND CULTURAL TRADITION AND THE NATIONAL CHARACTER OF THE BRITISH — precisely the same argument later used by the Qing 'conservatives'. And the height of the irony: THE RECENTLY TRANSLATED QING CODE WAS CITED BY THE SUPPORTERS OF REFORM AS A SOURCE OF INSPIRATION FOR IMPROVING BRITISH LAW AND BY THEIR OPPONENTS AS A CAUTIONARY EXAMPLE OF A CODIFIED SYSTEM UNSUITED TO A FREE AND 'MODERN' NATION SUCH AS BRITAIN. Although attempts to codify or 'modernise' the British common law largely failed over the next two centuries, BRITAIN'S STANDING AS A WORLD EMPIRE AND ITS CELEBRATED CODIFICATIONS FOR INDIA AND OTHER COLONIES led the founders of modern comparative law such as SIR HENRY MAINE AND MAX WEBER to place the British system in the family of the most advanced modern law. In other words: THE CENTURIES-OLD BRITISH LEGAL TRADITION SURVIVED THE MODERNISING IMPULSE OF THE 19TH CENTURY LARGELY INTACT AND EMERGED FROM IT AS THE MODEL MODERN LEGAL ORDER — in sharp contrast to the fate of the law of late imperial China.

cards.q: How was the Qing Code used in the British debates of 1810–1830?
cards.a: Both ways: the SUPPORTERS of reform cited it as a SOURCE OF INSPIRATION for improving British law, their OPPONENTS as a CAUTIONARY EXAMPLE of a codified system unsuited to a free and modern nation. The British debates meanwhile turned on the very same argument the Qing 'conservatives' would later use — whether reform suits the national character.

cards.q: Why did the British common law emerge from the 19th century as model modern law, although it was never successfully codified?
cards.a: Because of BRITAIN'S STANDING AS A WORLD EMPIRE and its celebrated codifications FOR INDIA and other colonies — on that basis the founders of comparative law such as Maine and Weber placed the British system in the family of the most advanced modern law. Standing, not content, decided the classification.

8.title: The strategy of bifurcation
8.text: The Chinese did resist the dominant discourse — and their principal instrument was BIFURCATION. They distinguished THE PRACTICAL MERITS OF AN INDIVIDUAL WESTERN LEGAL INSTITUTION FROM THE ALLEGED SUPERIORITY OF THE WESTERN TRADITION AS A WHOLE — and at the same time SEPARATED A REGRETTABLE ASPECT OR CASE OF CHINESE JUDICIAL PRACTICE FROM THE WHOLE CHINESE TRADITION. It is the analogue of the famous pairing ESSENCE (TI) AND FUNCTION (YONG) which late imperial intellectuals used for Western science: ONE COULD RECOMMEND ADOPTING A WESTERN INSTITUTION (function) IN THE SERVICE OF CHINESE ENDS (essence) WITHOUT ACCEPTING THE ORIENTALIST DISCOURSE OR CONCEDING CULTURAL OR RACIAL INFERIORITY. Further bifurcations: the difference between the THEORY AND THE PRACTICE of Western or Chinese law, and the difference between WESTERN METROPOLITAN RULE OF LAW AND JUSTICE IN THE WESTERN COLONIES OR EXTRATERRITORIAL COURTS. This allowed them to acknowledge the merits of Western theories and at the same time point to the GULF BETWEEN THOSE THEORIES AND WESTERN PRACTICE. A practical instance from 1881: Shenbao conceded that representation by counsel in the West limits manipulation by corrupt clerks, BUT WESTERN LAWYERS ARE NOT ALWAYS GUIDED BY IMPARTIALITY OR THE PUBLIC INTEREST — since both sides advocate for their clients, THE OUTCOME OF A DISPUTE MAY BE DETERMINED ENTIRELY BY THE RELATIVE SKILL OF THE LAWYERS, and a Western lawyer may therefore distort the facts and decide a case just as a corrupt Chinese clerk does. And the reverse symmetry Chen emphasises: BRITISH AND EUROPEAN COMMENTATORS USED A SIMILAR SET OF BIFURCATION STRATEGIES WHEN ASSESSING CHINESE LAW IN THE EARLY 19TH CENTURY. The Qing literati therefore differed in this respect not at all from their Western counterparts.

terms.def: The strategy of splitting: separating the practical merit of an individual foreign institution from the alleged superiority of the whole foreign tradition — and an individual domestic failing from the whole domestic tradition.
Essence and function: adopt a Western institution as function in the service of the Chinese essence, without conceding cultural inferiority.

cards.q: What is the strategy of bifurcation and what did it do for Qing authors?
cards.a: It separated the PRACTICAL MERIT of an individual Western institution from the ALLEGED SUPERIORITY of the Western tradition as a whole — and an individual Chinese failing from the whole Chinese tradition. It is the analogue of TI (essence) and YONG (function): one could adopt a Western institution in the service of Chinese ends without accepting the orientalist discourse or conceding inferiority.

cards.q: How did Shenbao question Western advocacy in 1881?
cards.a: It conceded that lawyers limit manipulation by corrupt clerks, but objected that they ARE NOT ALWAYS GUIDED BY IMPARTIALITY: since each advocates for his client, THE OUTCOME OF A DISPUTE MAY BE DETERMINED ENTIRELY BY THE RELATIVE SKILL OF THE LAWYERS — and a Western lawyer may therefore distort the facts just as a corrupt Chinese clerk does.

9.title: Essentialisation as a side effect of the defence
9.text: In trying to reconcile the adoption of foreign institutions with a claim to Chinese equality, however, the commentators ENDED UP ESSENTIALISING BOTH CHINESE AND WESTERN LEGAL CULTURE. According to one Shenbao article, LI (ritual propriety, moral norms) AND XING (law, punishment) WERE THE PAIRED PILLARS OF THE UNIVERSAL WAY OF GOVERNANCE; the Way is missing 'IF LI IS TOO RIGID AND XING TOO HARSH'. Under the norms of the time, officials had to kneel before the throne and litigants before the judge — which REIFIED AND WIDENED 'THE GULF BETWEEN SUPERIOR AND SUBORDINATE, SO THAT IT WAS DIFFICULT FOR THEM TO FEEL AFFECTION FOR ONE ANOTHER'. The lack of public support for the government in the recent Sino-Japanese dispute over Liuqiu was said to show that the existing ritual and judicial practice DID NOT CULTIVATE LOYALTY AND PATRIOTISM IN THE PEOPLE — and this was held to be the main difference between contemporary Chinese and Westerners. The authors thereby GAVE THE OLD CHINESE PAIRING OF LI AND XING A NEW MEANING AND POLITICAL FORCE, informed by international power politics and expressed in the WESTERN LANGUAGE OF INDIVIDUALISM, MODERNITY AND NATIONALISM. In doing so they NEUTRALISED PART OF THE EUROCENTRIC PREJUDICE and repackaged classical Chinese ideas of governance as universal values. BUT AT A PRICE: THEIR ARGUMENTS HAD THE EFFECT OF SIMPLIFYING THE LONG HISTORY AND THE CHANGING COMPLEXITIES OF CHINESE LAW AND CULTURE INTO ESSENTIALIST CONCEPTS AND CATEGORIES.

cards.q: What was the side effect of the Chinese defence against orientalism?
cards.a: ESSENTIALISATION. To defend their equality, Qing authors repackaged classical Chinese ideas (the pairing of LI and XING) as universal values and expressed them in the Western language of individualism, modernity and nationalism — which neutralised part of the Eurocentric prejudice but SIMPLIFIED THE LONG AND CHANGING HISTORY OF CHINESE LAW INTO ESSENTIALIST CATEGORIES.

10.title: How a promise became a treaty obligation
10.text: A timeline worth knowing precisely. The British and the other powers did not make THE WESTERNISATION OF CHINESE LAW A CONDITION of surrendering extraterritoriality UNTIL THE 1860s. When the Anglo-American governments insisted that their nationals should have the same privileges as the Chinese to travel, trade and reside in the interior, PRINCE GONG replied at the end of 1868 that foreigners could have those privileges IF THEY SUBMITTED TO CHINESE LAW AS CHINESE SUBJECTS DID. The American minister ROSS BROWNE insisted that China must first establish a 'CODE FOUNDED UPON PRINCIPLES OF JUSTICE, RECOGNISED AND ACCEPTED BY THE COMMUNITY OF WESTERN NATIONS, TO WHICH THE GOVERNMENT OF THE UNITED STATES CAN SAFELY GIVE ITS ASSENT'; the British minister ALCOCK repeated it. In December 1868 the Qing government promised to adopt 'A WRITTEN CODE OF COMMERCIAL LAW AND FIXED RULES OF PROCEDURE AND PRACTICE'. And the American minister's words were entirely open: it was necessary to 'FORCE OUR CIVILISATION UPON THEM… TO ADVANCE THEM TO A HIGHER CIVILISATION'. And then: AFTER THE SIGNING OF THE BOXER PROTOCOL IN 1901 THE PROMISE OF 1868 TURNED INTO A TREATY OBLIGATION, worded in such a way as to give the impression THAT CHINA DESIRED THE WESTERNISATION OF ITS LAW VOLUNTARILY AND OF ITS OWN ACCORD. ARTICLE XII of the Sino-British commercial treaty of 1902: 'CHINA HAVING EXPRESSED A STRONG DESIRE TO REFORM HER JUDICIAL SYSTEM AND TO BRING IT INTO ACCORD WITH THAT OF WESTERN NATIONS, GREAT BRITAIN AGREES TO GIVE EVERY ASSISTANCE TO SUCH REFORM, AND SHE WILL ALSO BE PREPARED TO RELINQUISH HER EXTRATERRITORIAL RIGHTS WHEN SHE IS SATISFIED THAT THE STATE OF THE CHINESE LAWS, THE ARRANGEMENT FOR THEIR ADMINISTRATION AND OTHER CONSIDERATIONS WARRANT HER IN SO DOING.' Read carefully who decides: THE FOREIGN POWERS THEMSELVES DETERMINED WHETHER AND WHEN THEY WOULD SURRENDER EXTRATERRITORIALITY — and despite enormous changes over the next two decades they expressed dissatisfaction and GAVE IT UP ONLY IN 1943, WHEN THE SECOND WORLD WAR FORCED THEM TO.

cards.q: How was the reform obligation worded in the Sino-British treaty of 1902, and why does the wording matter?
cards.a: 'China having expressed a STRONG DESIRE to reform her judicial system… Great Britain will be prepared to relinquish her extraterritorial rights WHEN SHE IS SATISFIED that the state of the Chinese laws warrants her in so doing.' It matters twice over: it gives the impression that China wants westernisation VOLUNTARILY, and the decision as to when the reform is good enough is reserved to THE POWERS THEMSELVES.

cards.q: When did the powers actually give up extraterritoriality in China?
cards.a: ONLY IN 1943, when the Second World War forced them to — despite the enormous changes in the Chinese legal order over the preceding two decades, with which the powers continued to express dissatisfaction. Lao Naixuan had already argued correctly in 1910 that legal reform alone would not decide the abolition of extraterritoriality.

11.title: The reform of 1902–1911: what actually happened
11.text: After the suppression of the Boxer Uprising and the occupation of Beijing by eight powers in 1900, the Manchu court fled to Xi'an and at the beginning of 1901 issued an edict inviting proposals from senior officials. In 1902 THREE MEMORIALS submitted by the governors ZHANG ZHIDONG and LIU KUNYI, calling for comprehensive reform, were approved. The proposed changes in law: REDUCE LITIGATION AND BUREAUCRACY, MITIGATE PUNISHMENTS, BUILD PRISONS, CONVERT CORPORAL PUNISHMENTS INTO MONETARY FINES AND SEPARATE ADMINISTRATIVE FROM JUDICIAL DUTIES. Over the following decade the COMMISSION FOR THE REVISION OF LAWS (established 1904) and the COMMISSION FOR DRAFTING THE CONSTITUTION launched a series of programmes: sending students abroad, founding law schools, recruiting foreign and foreign-trained Chinese jurists, and translating foreign codes. By 1911 these produced DRAFTS of civil, criminal, procedural, nationality, press and copyright codes. One inconspicuous but fundamental change: THE CENTURIES-OLD PRACTICE OF ARRANGING THE CONTENT OF THE DYNASTIC CODES ACCORDING TO THE SIX MINISTRIES WAS REPLACED BY THE WESTERN DIVISION INTO CIVIL, PROCEDURAL, CRIMINAL, COMMERCIAL AND CONSTITUTIONAL LAW. And Chen adds why: Western commentators on Staunton's translation criticised the Chinese order for its allegedly IRRATIONAL STRUCTURE AND ITS LACK OF CIVIL LAW, LEGAL CONSCIOUSNESS AND INDIVIDUAL FREEDOM — and THE REFORMERS, ANXIOUS TO MEET FOREIGN EXPECTATIONS, OFTEN MADE THOSE STEREOTYPICAL CHARACTERISATIONS INDISPUTABLE AND SELF-FULFILLING. In 1902 the reformers also, at the first opportunity, ABOLISHED THE THREE HEAVIEST PUNISHMENTS — SLICING (LINGCHI), THE DISPLAY OF THE HEAD (XIAOSHOU) AND THE DESECRATION OF THE CORPSE (LUSHI) — and also TATTOOING AND VICARIOUS CRIMINAL LIABILITY (YUANZUO); JUDICIAL TORTURE was prohibited except in capital cases where guilt had already been established by several witnesses.

cards.q: Which punishments did the late Qing abolish in 1902, and why precisely those?
cards.a: Slicing (lingchi), the display of the severed head (xiaoshou), the desecration of the corpse (lushi), tattooing and vicarious criminal liability (yuanzuo); judicial torture was prohibited except in capital cases with several witnesses. Precisely those because EURO-AMERICANS HAD CITED THEM SINCE THE 18TH CENTURY TO STIGMATISE CHINESE LAW — often retrospectively, to justify their own circumvention of Chinese jurisdiction.

cards.q: How did the reform change the very arrangement of the code, and what does that illustrate?
cards.a: The centuries-old practice of arranging the content by the SIX MINISTRIES was replaced by the Western division into civil, procedural, criminal, commercial and constitutional law. It illustrates Chen's thesis: Western criticism reproached the Chinese order for an irrational structure and a missing civil law, and the reformers, anxious to meet foreign expectations, MADE THOSE STEREOTYPES INDISPUTABLE AND SELF-FULFILLING.

12.title: Shen Jiaben: the moderate path and the argument from sovereignty
12.text: An edict of May 1902 appointed as commissioners for the revision of law SHEN JIABEN (the leading Qing jurist) and WU TINGFANG (the first Chinese trained as a barrister in England), with instructions to 'STUDY THE LAWS OF ALL COUNTRIES' and create an order 'APPLICABLE TO CHINESE AND FOREIGNERS ALIKE'. The new draft criminal code of 1906 sought to CONVERT CORPORAL PUNISHMENTS INTO THE DEATH PENALTY (by strangulation only), IMPRISONMENT, DETENTION AND FINES; to REDUCE THE NUMBER OF CAPITAL PROVISIONS; to ABOLISH ADJUDICATION BY ANALOGY (BIFU) where a provision was lacking; and to BUILD CORRECTIONAL FACILITIES FOR JUVENILES. Shen justified this by CITATIONS FROM THE CHINESE LAW OF EARLIER DYNASTIES as well as from contemporary Western systems, thereby portraying the existing laws as contrary both to THE BETTER CHINESE TRADITION AND to the 'UNIVERSAL' PRACTICE OF THE MODERN WORLD. And his main argument to the court was one of sovereignty: 'AN INDEPENDENT STATE SHOULD HAVE EXCLUSIVE JURISDICTION (DULI FAQUAN) OVER ITS TERRITORY. APART FROM FOREIGN SOVEREIGNS, DIPLOMATS AND CERTAIN TROOPS, ALL FOREIGNERS ARE SUBJECT TO THE LAW OF THE COUNTRY UNDER INTERNATIONAL NORMS. CONSULAR JURISDICTION, HOWEVER, WAS INTRODUCED IN CHINA ON THE PRETEXT THAT OUR JUDICIAL ORDER IS DEFECTIVE. BRITAIN BEGAN IT AND GERMANY FOLLOWED, WHILE JAPAN HAS EVEN ESTABLISHED COURTS IN THE ANCESTRAL HOMELAND [OF THE QING RULERS IN MANCHURIA]. OUR SOVEREIGNTY IS BEING UNDERMINED DAY BY DAY.' Beside Shen stood JI TONGJUN, who apparently was the first to recommend abolishing the cruel corporal punishments, but whose ideal was TO REVISE THE QING ORDER WITHOUT ABANDONING ITS ESSENCE — he therefore secured the adaptation of the Qing code into the CRIMINAL LAW IN FORCE (XIANXING XINGLÜ). Shen and Ji agreed that THE ESSENCE OF CHINESE LAW IS NOT INCOMMENSURABLE WITH WESTERN OR MODERN LAW AND THAT CHINESE MODERNITY CANNOT AND SHOULD NOT ARISE FROM THE COMPLETE DECONSTRUCTION OR DESTRUCTION OF THE CHINESE LEGAL TRADITION.

cards.q: What was Shen Jiaben's main argument for reform?
cards.a: SOVEREIGNTY: 'An independent state should have exclusive jurisdiction over its territory. Apart from foreign sovereigns, diplomats and certain troops, all foreigners are subject to the law of the country under international norms. Consular jurisdiction, however, was introduced in China ON THE PRETEXT that our judicial order is defective… Our sovereignty is being undermined day by day.'

cards.q: How did Shen Jiaben justify the proposed changes?
cards.a: In two ways at once: by CITATIONS FROM THE CHINESE LAW OF EARLIER DYNASTIES and from contemporary Western systems, thereby portraying the existing laws as contrary both to THE BETTER CHINESE TRADITION and to the 'universal' practice of the modern world. It was a moderate middle path between clinging to the existing order and taking westernisation for granted.

13.title: The quarrel over the new criminal code: familism against statism
13.text: The draft of the new criminal code was prepared in 1906–07 by the hired Japanese professor of criminal law OKADA ASATARO on the model of the JAPANESE CRIMINAL CODE, itself modelled on Western examples; he was assisted by graduates of Japanese law schools. Between 1908 and 1910 some TWO DOZEN MEMORIALS came in: the commentators shared the sense of urgency about reform, but many held that THE DRAFT HAD GONE TOO FAR IN ADOPTING A FOREIGN CODE WITHOUT REGARD FOR THE HIERARCHICAL SOCIAL AND POLITICAL ORDER (SANGANG WUCHANG) AND THE MORAL NORMS (LIJIAO). Particularly severe was the memorial of the MINISTRY OF EDUCATION under Zhang Zhidong, attacking the new code for ABOLISHING THE DIFFERENTIATED LEGAL TREATMENT OF PEOPLE ACCORDING TO SOCIAL, FAMILIAL AND GENDER STATUS. And the central formulation of the dispute comes from YANG DU, who had studied in Japan: THE DEBATE IS NOT MERELY ABOUT A CODE, BUT ABOUT WHETHER CHINA SHOULD REPLACE ITS OLD 'FAMILISM' (JIATING ZHUYI) WITH THE 'STATISM' (GUOJIA ZHUYI) PREVAILING ELSEWHERE. On his view, Chinese weakness followed from the fact that its laws and moral norms ARE ROOTED IN FAMILISM, IN WHICH EVERY INDIVIDUAL'S RIGHTS AND DUTIES ARE TIED TO THE FAMILY INSTEAD OF THE STATE — whereas elsewhere they are rooted in statism, in which EVERY ADULT BECOMES A CITIZEN OF THE COUNTRY (GUOMIN) and his wealth and abilities are converted into national strength. Chen adds that Yang probably encountered the translation of MAINE'S ANCIENT LAW (1861), which Liang Qichao expressly cited at the same period: Maine argued that China had never moved beyond a society based on STATUS towards a society based on CONTRACT, and that while law had helped other societies forward, CHINESE LAW HELD THAT COUNTRY BACK.

terms.def: Yang Du's formulation of the dispute: are an individual's rights and duties tied to the FAMILY, or to the STATE of which he is a citizen (guomin)?

cards.q: How did Yang Du formulate the core of the dispute over the new criminal code?
cards.a: That it was not merely about a code but about WHETHER CHINA SHOULD REPLACE ITS OLD 'FAMILISM' (jiating zhuyi) WITH 'STATISM' (guojia zhuyi). Under familism an individual's rights and duties are tied to the FAMILY; under statism every adult becomes a CITIZEN OF THE COUNTRY (guomin) and his abilities are converted into national strength.

cards.q: What did Henry Maine claim about China, and how did it fit into the Qing debate?
cards.a: That China had never moved beyond a society based on STATUS towards a society based on CONTRACT, and that while law had helped other societies forward, CHINESE LAW HELD THE COUNTRY BACK. Yang Du probably encountered the translation of Ancient Law and Liang Qichao cited it expressly at the same time — Western comparative law thus supplied Chinese reformers with an argument against their own tradition.

14.title: Lao Naixuan: the 'conservative' who agreed with 97 per cent
14.text: LAO NAIXUAN, the leading critical voice, has been criticised for a whole century as an irrational conservative clinging to a backward tradition — and Chen shows that the label MISSES THE COMPLEXITY OF THE CHINESE EXPERIENCE OF MODERNITY. Lao and his supporters, who made up MORE THAN HALF THE MEMBERS OF THE IMPERIAL ASSEMBLY, in fact REJECTED NEITHER MOST OF THE NEW CODE NOR THE REFORM MOVEMENT ITSELF. Lao agreed that reform was necessary to abolish extraterritoriality; HE WAS NOT AGAINST ABOLISHING THE BAMBOO BEATING AND JUDICIAL TORTURE, NOR AGAINST INTRODUCING JUDICIAL INDEPENDENCE AND A PRISON SYSTEM. What was contested was Yang Du's claim that China must adopt THE SAME KIND of system as Japan and the West. Lao's arguments are worth remembering because they sound eminently reasonable. FIRST: once those reforms were carried out, China would meet the conditions of the treaties, PROVIDED THE REFORMED ORDER WAS 'BROADLY COMPARABLE' (DATI XIANGTONG) with the orders of the extraterritorial powers. SECOND, to those who demanded that almost every article should satisfy foreigners: THE EXTRATERRITORIAL POWERS THEMSELVES DIFFER FROM ONE ANOTHER IN VARIOUS RESPECTS, so it is IMPOSSIBLE to satisfy them all. THIRD: AMONG THE TREATY POWERS, THE NATIONALS OF ONE COUNTRY CANNOT REFUSE THE JURISDICTION OF ANOTHER MERELY BECAUSE ITS LAW DIFFERS FROM THEIRS. FOURTH, from his own experience of foreign governments: LEGAL REFORM ALONE WILL NOT DECIDE THE ABOLITION OF EXTRATERRITORIALITY. And Chen adds: HE WAS RIGHT ABOUT THAT — extraterritoriality ended three decades after the Qing reform. Lao himself complained that the press attacked him as the public enemy of the new code, although HE SUPPORTED OVER 97 PER CENT OF ITS FOUR HUNDRED ARTICLES and asked only for five or six articles to be restored or amended and eight or nine added.

cards.q: What four arguments did Lao Naixuan raise against the demand for complete westernisation?
cards.a: 1) It would suffice for the reformed order to be 'BROADLY COMPARABLE' (dati xiangtong) with those of the powers. 2) The powers themselves differ from one another, so satisfying them all is impossible. 3) Among the treaty powers the nationals of one country cannot refuse another's jurisdiction merely because its law differs. 4) Legal reform alone will not decide the abolition of extraterritoriality — and in this he was right, it ended only in 1943.

cards.q: Was Lao Naixuan an opponent of reform?
cards.a: He was not. HE SUPPORTED OVER 97 PER CENT of the four hundred articles of the new code, asking only for five or six to be restored or amended and eight or nine added; he was not against abolishing the bamboo beating or judicial torture, nor against judicial independence and a prison system. The press nevertheless portrayed him as the public enemy of the new code.

15.title: The dispute reduced to two questions
15.text: Lao, however, ESSENTIALISED AS WELL. Rather than attacking the new code for its foreign roots, he sought to RESTORE SEVERAL QING PROVISIONS to it: on crimes between relatives, on digging up other people's graves, on the FORNICATION OF UNMARRIED WOMEN (WU FU JIAN) and on the RIGHT TO DISCIPLINE CHILDREN AND GRANDCHILDREN. He regarded those provisions as fundamental to the social order and moral norms (LUNJI LIJIAO), and therefore indispensable. Unlike Yang Du, he did not think LAW AND MORALITY COULD BE COMPLETELY SEPARATED. He accepted Yang's claim that China rests on the spirit of familism, BUT HE ATTRIBUTED THE LACK OF NATIONAL CONSCIOUSNESS AND PATRIOTISM NOT TO LAW OR TO FAMILISM BUT TO THE POLITICAL INSTITUTIONS OF 'DESPOTISM' (ZHUANZHI ZHUYI). Setting China as an agrarian society against the Western industrial nations, he concluded that THE WAY AND CONDITIONS OF A NATION'S LIFE DETERMINE ITS CUSTOMS, MORAL NORMS AND INSTITUTIONS, AND ONLY THEN ITS LAW (he divided societies into three types: agrarian, governed by family law; nomadic, by military law; industrial, by commercial law). By the end of the first reading the dispute had been REDUCED TO TWO QUESTIONS: 1) SHOULD THE CODE PUNISH THE FORNICATION OF UNMARRIED WOMEN? 2) SHOULD IT PUNISH INJURING A CHILD OR GRANDCHILD WHILE DISCIPLINING HIM AS THOUGH IT WERE AN INJURY BETWEEN EQUALS (ZISUN WEIFAN JIAOLING)? Shen Jiaben and his people argued that these were NOT LEGAL BUT MORAL questions belonging to education; Lao and Chen Baochen held them to be crucial to public morality and therefore worthy of state intervention. For several weeks this inflamed the public in Tianjin, Shanghai and Beijing; the newspapers usually flogged Lao's 'faction' as a reactionary obstacle to progress, and tempers rose so high that GAO LINGXIAO, a vocal supporter of Lao, EVEN EXCHANGED BLOWS with supporters of the new code in front of the assembly.

cards.q: To which two questions was the dispute over the criminal code finally reduced?
cards.a: 1) Whether the code should punish the FORNICATION OF UNMARRIED WOMEN. 2) Whether it should punish INJURING A CHILD OR GRANDCHILD WHILE DISCIPLINING HIM as though it were an injury between equals. Shen Jiaben regarded these as moral, not legal, questions belonging to education; Lao and Chen Baochen as crucial to public morality and therefore fit for state intervention.

cards.q: To what did Lao Naixuan attribute the lack of Chinese national consciousness?
cards.a: Not to law or to familism, but to the POLITICAL INSTITUTIONS OF 'DESPOTISM' (zhuanzhi zhuyi). He argued that the way and conditions of a nation's life determine its customs, moral norms and institutions, and only then its law — dividing societies into agrarian (family law), nomadic (military law) and industrial (commercial law).

16.title: The irony at the end: foreigners defend the Chinese tradition
16.text: At the close of the Qing era it was JURISTS FROM THE TREATY POWERS who acknowledged the value of the dying Chinese legal tradition. The German jurist DR HARALD GUTHERZ, lecturing at the Sino-German Institute in Qingdao, wrote a famous critique of the new criminal code in 1910 warning THAT THE CHINESE SHOULD NOT WHOLLY ABANDON THEIR OWN LEGAL ORDER IN FAVOUR OF A FOREIGN ONE, BECAUSE EUROPEAN JURISTS TOO HAD ACKNOWLEDGED THE MERITS OF THE QING CODE EVER SINCE STAUNTON'S TRANSLATION OF 1810. And CHARLES SUMNER LOBINGER, judge of the American extraterritorial court in Shanghai, reminded his readers in 1908 of the forgotten fact that China had A HIGHLY SOPHISTICATED LEGAL ORDER AND BY FAR THE OLDEST CONTINUOUSLY OPERATIVE CODE IN THE WORLD — remarking that IF JUSTINIAN'S CODE HAD BEEN IN FORCE SINCE ITS PROMULGATION IN THE 6TH CENTURY, IT WOULD STILL BE VERY YOUNG BY COMPARISON WITH THE CHINESE ONE.

cards.q: Who defended the value of the Chinese legal tradition at the end of the Qing era?
cards.a: JURISTS FROM THE TREATY POWERS. The German jurist Harald Gutherz warned in 1910 that the Chinese should not wholly abandon their own order, since European jurists had acknowledged the merits of the Qing Code ever since Staunton's translation. And the American judge Charles Sumner Lobinger recalled in 1908 that China had the oldest continuously operative code in the world — against which Justinian's Code would still be very young.

17.title: The reformers who changed their minds
17.text: The strongest evidence for Chen's thesis. WANG RONGBAO, one of the drafters and defenders of the new code, in 1927 essentially admitted a mistake seventeen years old. He acknowledged that late imperial Chinese law HAD GROWN ORGANICALLY OUT OF A LONG HISTORY AND HAD ALREADY DEVELOPED BY THE TANG PERIOD IN THE 7TH CENTURY INTO A SOPHISTICATED ORDER COMPARABLE WITH THE WESTERN ONE. And his reason for having supported it so zealously at the time is highly instructive: 'THE NEW CRIMINAL CODE ADOPTED A GREAT MANY WESTERN LEGAL IDEAS, IN SHARP CONTRAST TO OLD CHINESE LAW. I OFTEN THOUGHT THIS PROBLEMATIC (CHANG YIWEI BIN), BUT I COULD NOT HAVE DISAGREED WITH THE OTHERS EVEN HAD I WISHED TO, BECAUSE IT [THE DESIRE TO WESTERNISE CHINESE LAW] FOLLOWED FROM THE PREVAILING MOOD (FENGHUI) OF THE TIME AND FROM THE EXAMPLES OF NUMEROUS FOREIGN COUNTRIES.' In 1926 Wang then repeated what Lao had said in 1910: FA AND LI ARE TWO SIDES OF THE SAME COIN AND ARE 'MUTUALLY INTERCHANGEABLE' — and he went even further than Lao in claiming that THE RULE OF LAW IS IN ESSENCE THE RULE OF LI and that foreign-educated Chinese insisted on separating them because THEIR KNOWLEDGE WAS SUPERFICIAL AND THEY DID NOT UNDERSTAND THE ORIGIN OF LAW. DONG KANG, another defender of 1910, also changed his mind: at the time he had argued that the existing order could not be preserved if China was to 'advance and prosper' and avoid the sorry fate of Turkey and India; ten years later he ATTRIBUTED HIS EARLIER DISMISSIVE STANCE TO THE INFLUENCE OF WESTERN IDEAS and concluded that reform could not proceed by abandoning Chinese LIJIAO, since that would be like 'CUTTING OFF THE FEET TO FIT THE SHOES'.

cards.q: Why did Wang Rongbao in 1910 support a code he inwardly disagreed with?
cards.a: In his own words from 1927: 'I often thought this problematic, BUT I COULD NOT HAVE DISAGREED WITH THE OTHERS EVEN HAD I WISHED TO, BECAUSE IT FOLLOWED FROM THE PREVAILING MOOD OF THE TIME AND FROM THE EXAMPLES OF NUMEROUS FOREIGN COUNTRIES.' It is the most direct evidence of symbolic violence: the pressure of the discourse worked even on those who were spreading it.

cards.q: What did Dong Kang later think of his position of 1910?
cards.a: At the time he argued that the existing Chinese order could not be preserved if China was to advance and avoid the fate of Turkey and India. Ten years later he ATTRIBUTED HIS DISMISSIVE STANCE TO THE INFLUENCE OF WESTERN IDEAS and concluded that reform could not proceed by abandoning Chinese LIJIAO, since that would be like 'cutting off the feet to fit the shoes'.

18.title: Conclusion: the die was cast
18.text: And yet — even in those later self-reflections Wang and Dong CONTINUED TO DISPLAY THE EFFECT OF THE SYMBOLIC VIOLENCE OF CULTURAL IMPERIALISM, because they went on using a self-orientalising language that REDUCED THE CHINESE LEGAL TRADITION AND SOCIAL REALITY TO LIJIAO, THE FAMILY AND SOCIAL HIERARCHY ALONE. As the historian ARIF DIRLIK observed, this essentialism was meant to repel complete westernisation but 'IN THE VERY PROCESS ALSO CONSOLIDATED „WESTERN“ IDEOLOGICAL HEGEMONY BY INTERNALISING THE HISTORICAL ASSUMPTIONS OF ORIENTALISM'. Although some reformers changed their minds, THE DIE HAD ALREADY BEEN CAST: they had made Chinese law an ORIENTAL LEGAL TRADITION PRESUMED TO BE THE OPPOSITE OF MODERN LAW. BY THE EARLY 1930s THE LEGAL ORDER THAT HAD GOVERNED IMPERIAL CHINA FOR MORE THAN A THOUSAND YEARS COULD SCARCELY CLAIM ANY LEGITIMATE ROLE IN A NOW 'MODERN' COUNTRY. By contrast, THE ANGLO-AMERICAN LEGAL TRADITION, WHOSE HISTORY STRETCHES ACROSS MANY CENTURIES, BECAME PART OF THE UNIVERSAL STANDARD DEFINING MODERN LAW EVEN IN THE 21ST CENTURY. The closing theses: the history of the Chinese reforms CANNOT BE REDUCED TO NEAT DICHOTOMIES of tradition and modernity, China and the West, success and failure, conservative and progressive; THE 'CONSERVATIVES' AND THE 'REFORMERS' HAD MORE IN COMMON THAN HAS BEEN ACKNOWLEDGED, and BOTH SIDES made essentialising characterisations. And a final sentence worth knowing: THE HISTORY OF CHINESE LEGAL MODERNITY MUST BE UNDERSTOOD AS A CONSTANT STRUGGLE FOR BALANCE BETWEEN ANXIETY ABOUT CULTURAL IDENTITY AND THE DESIRE FOR INTERNATIONAL RECOGNITION FROM THE DOMINANT POWERS — AND UNTIL THAT FRAGILE BALANCE IS FOUND, THE CHINESE LEGAL ORDER WILL APPEAR TOO FOREIGN TO THE CHINESE AND TOO CHINESE TO FOREIGNERS.

cards.q: How does Dirlik assess the essentialism with which the Chinese resisted westernisation?
cards.a: That it was meant to repel complete westernisation but 'IN THE VERY PROCESS ALSO CONSOLIDATED „WESTERN“ IDEOLOGICAL HEGEMONY BY INTERNALISING THE HISTORICAL ASSUMPTIONS OF ORIENTALISM'. The defence took over the very framework it was defending against.

cards.q: Sum up Chen's conclusion about the history of Chinese legal modernity.
cards.a: It cannot be reduced to neat dichotomies of tradition/modernity, China/West, success/failure; the 'conservatives' and the 'reformers' had more in common than has been acknowledged, and BOTH sides essentialised. It is a CONSTANT STRUGGLE FOR BALANCE BETWEEN ANXIETY ABOUT CULTURAL IDENTITY AND THE DESIRE FOR INTERNATIONAL RECOGNITION — and until that balance is found, the Chinese order will appear too foreign to the Chinese and too Chinese to foreigners.
